Pitching has been a major strength for the New York Yankees this season, particularly starting pitching. But the Yankees have dealt with numerous pitching injuries with Max Fried (two stints on the IL), Carlos Rodón (two stints on the IL), Ryan Weathers (currently on the IL) and Fernando Cruz (currently on the IL) all going down at certain points of the season. Not to mention, Gerrit Cole and Clarke Schmidt missed time this year while recovering from Tommy John surgery, and Rodón didn't make his season debut until May due to offseason surgery.
So it remains to be seen whether the Yankees' pitching staff will be able to hold up for a deep postseason run. And on Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins, Rodón initially gave Yankees fans cause for concern.
Rodón's concerning dip in velocity vs. Twins
Rodón's fastball velocity was down in the low-90s across the first three innings of his most recent start in Minnesota. The left-hander threw some fastballs at 90 mph to begin the game and averaged 92.6 mph on the pitch, as opposed to his season average of 94.4 mph.
Luckily, Rodón was able to crank things up in his final three innings of work, throwing a number of pitches above 95 mph afterwards. This likely made the Yankees and their fans breathe a sigh of relief for the time being. But Rodón's explanation after the game won't give fans much clarity.
Rodón's explanation
According to Gary Phillips of The New York Daily News, Rodón told reporters that he was dealing with tightness at the beginning of his start, but was able to get loose as his outing progressed. Rodón didn't specify where he was feeling tight/whether it was localized or if he was just trying to say he felt a generalized sense that he couldn't break through the way he wanted to.
So while it's good news that Rodón was able to shake it off after the third, the Yankees should still be worried about his overall durability with the postseason around the corner. Rodón is slated to be the Yankees' No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Cam Schlittler, Cole and Fried. They will have to hope that his tightness doesn't come back in his next start or in the postseason or snowball into something worse.
As aforementioned, Rodón was out until May of this season after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur from his left elbow last October. He also dealt with a hamstring issue during his rehab. In addition to his initial IL stint, Rodón missed over a month and a half of action from Jun. 28 to Aug. 18 with left elbow inflammation. The 33-year-old has pitched very well in 15 starts this season (2.95 ERA), but this latest blip should have the Yankees questioning whether they can rely on him the rest of the way.

PHOENIX — There always was the understanding that there would be some bumps along the road in Gerrit Cole’s first season back from Tommy John surgery, as there are with any pitcher returning from major elbow surgery. Yet, for most of his first 20 starts back, he looked like the Cole of old.
The last two, however, have started to ring some moderate alarm bells at an inopportune time — or, if viewed through the Yankees’ pinstriped glasses, a decent time so that he can get himself straightened out over his final two starts before the playoffs.

That quest begins Friday, when Cole will take the mound against the Diamondbacks having allowed seven home runs over his last two starts, the most in any two-start span of his career.
“I expect him to be right next time,” manager Aaron Boone said after Cole’s last start against the Mets.
Cole has insisted throughout that he is feeling good physically, 115 ¹/₃ innings into the season after missing all of last year.
The metrics on his pitches over the last two starts against the Mets and Padres have mostly stayed in line with where they have been over the course of the full season, including his fastball velocity, which averaged 97.1 mph and 96.9 mph in those two starts (both faster than his season average in 2024).
Except all of a sudden, that four-seam fastball has become a lot more hittable. Dating back to Cole’s last four starts, hitters are batting 16-for-48 (.333) against the pitch, compared to 32-for-173 (.185) across his first 16 starts. Perhaps even more concerning is that hitters are not just hitting the fastball — they are hardly even missing it.
Over his last three starts, Cole has generated just eight whiffs on 69 swings against his fastball (11.6 percent), including zero on 16 swings last time out against the Mets, compared to a 22.8 percent whiff rate on the pitch in his first 17 starts (which is still down from the rest of his career).
Former American League Cy Young Award winner and current YES Network analyst David Cone, speaking this week on “The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman,” theorized that Cole often has been in between on which secondary pitch to use, which has allowed hitters to wait and attack his fastball.
“To me, that just leans back to they’re not respecting your secondary stuff, they’re sitting on your fastball,” Cone said. “You got to get some protection for your fastball, and you got to do something about your secondary pitches and get your slider tunneling again on that same plane off of that fastball. That will give you what you’re looking for.”
Of the seven home runs Cole has given up in his last two starts, four have come on his fastball.
During those two starts, hitters have put 22 fastballs in play, with 15 of them registering as hard-hit balls, meaning they have come off the bat at exit velocities north of 95 mph. The average exit velocity on Cole’s fastballs during those two starts has been 98.3, compared to 92.7 in his first 18 starts.
All of that suggests that hitters are seeing Cole’s fastball well. Whether that is because of a lack of deception, he is not getting it to the spots he wants, or they simply are sitting fastball and unleashing their best swings when they get it is a matter of opinion.
Shop Yankees Merch
Now, it is on Cole to adjust back in his final two starts of the regular season (lined up to come against the Diamondbacks and Rays). Prior to the clunkers against the Padres and Mets, he had pitched to 3.29 ERA across 18 starts, looking very much like the kind of pitcher the Yankees would want to start in a potential AL wild-card series along with Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
While the concerning last two starts probably still are not enough to make the Yankees change course and start Carlos Rodón over him, Cole could go a long way in offering some reassurance by solving his home run and fastball problem before the postseason arrives.

It wouldn't have been a proper Yankees-Twins series in Minnesota without a game that devolved into extra-innings madness. The Yankees failed to cash in multiple bases loaded opportunities and so missed a chance to sweep, falling farther behind the Rays in the standings. Nonetheless, the Bombers took care of business in the first two games of the series, and it is from the middle game that we pull our candidate for Sequence of the Week.
We join Max Fried with two outs in the bottom of the fifth on Tuesday at Target Field. The Yankees have a 3-1 lead courtesy of a Cody Bellinger two-run homer and George Lombard Jr. RBI single. However, the Twins are threatening to cut the lead to one with Emmanuel Rodriguez on second with a two-out double. That brings the number nine hitter Austin Martin to the plate, a batter Fried absolutely wants to retire to avoid the lineup turning over with a runner in scoring position.
After going almost all fastballs the first time he faced Martin, Fried looks to steal a called first-pitch strike with a backdoor sweeper.
After seeing mostly hard stuff that moved away from him, you can understand why Martin would give up on this pitch early given how far from the strike zone it is initially aimed. Fried sweeps in a dandy on the outer half for called strike one.
Establishing that backdoor breaking ball for a called strike forces Martin to respect any pitches that start away, even those that look like balls out of the hand. This opens up a host of possibilities for Fried, including the changeup low and away for chase.
This is a pretty well-executed changeup out of the zone down and outside. It looks like it is aimed at that corner of the zone before fading away from the hitter. You can see Martin was initially tempted to chase the pitch — a product of that first pitch backdoor sweeper — before holding up for an impressively disciplined take.
With Martin taking against that last pitch away, Fried and Ali Sánchez feel that there is an opening for another backdoor sweeper.
Another decently executed pitch, just a little too low to nip the bottom of the zone for a second called strike. It is worth noting that Martin showed some willingness to offer before backing off, so that outside pitch is still open for chase opportunities.
Not wanting to fall any further behind in the count, Fried throws his first fastball of the encounter. However, unlike the four-seamers and sinkers he threw Martin in the first AB, this cutter breaks toward the hitter instead of away. Therefore, if the hitter succeeds in reading fastball spin out of the hand, a backdoor cutter that starts off the plate away should freeze Martin.
That is precisely what happens, Fried pinpointing this cutter with precision on the corner up and away. Martin leaves the bat on his shoulder, only to watch the pitch cut across the black of the plate for called strike two.
Now that he has established his fastball in the zone and has the count leverage in his favor, Fried has an opening to climb the ladder with the cutter hoping for a chase and whiff under a pitch elevated above the zone.
Even though this offering misses the top of the zone by about a foot, it's not a complete waste pitch. Fried has reset the hitter's eye level for the fastball up, which should open the door for a breaking ball down and in.
That is just what Fried's thought process is with the count full. He doesn't need to give in with a fastball with first base open, knowing that it will be very hard for Martin to lay off a breaking ball that looks like a strike out of the hand.
Now this is what you call a back-foot sweeper. The pitch looks like a strike for much of its journey toward home until the lateral sweep really seems to accelerate in the final 15 feet. It's just where you want to land a pitch like this, close enough to the strike zone to extract the chase but close enough to the batter that he is not able to pull in his hands in time to make contact.
Here's the full sequence:
Asked after the start what positives he would take away, Fried cited breaking ball command and an economical pitch count to go seven strong on just 88 pitches, the first point certainly highlighted by this sequence.
The Yankees desperately needed this start from Fried, not only to boost their chances of winning this particular game but also as a sign of continued build-up from the recurrence of his left elbow bone bruise. Fried labored in the start before this one, needing 80 pitches to complete 3.1 innings. Seeing him back to his best when it comes to pitch efficiency and damage limitation has to be encouraging as they formulate their postseason rotation plans.

There is a point where a nice stretch stops being a nice stretch. Carlos Rodón has crossed that line for the Yankees.
Rodón gave them six innings, two earned runs and five strikeouts on Wednesday in Minnesota. The 5-4 loss took some shine off the afternoon, but his start extended a run that is getting hard to brush aside: 25 straight outings with no more than three runs allowed and no more than one homer surrendered.
He does not have to start Game 1. Max Fried and Cam Schlittler have been excellent, and October is not a participation trophy for everybody who had a good September. The rotation conversation cannot be handled with old assumptions anymore.
The Yankees have a real surplus of starters who can make a case. It is a good issue to have, but the first series is short and the opponent decides who gets the ball after the opener.
The Yankees have to count the whole body of work
Rodón’s recent run is not built on smoke. He has kept the ball in the yard, limited crooked innings, and worked deep enough into games to spare the bullpen. Wednesday was not perfect, with three walks and 102 pitches, yet he gave New York a clean six-inning start while the game was still there for the taking.
October asks for exactly that kind of start. Nobody needs a masterpiece every time; they need someone who can keep a game in the middle innings without handing the other dugout a free runway.
I would not overreact to one loss in Minneapolis. I would react to the 25-start sample, because it now carries real weight in the Yankees’ season.
Carlos Rodón has earned a real say in October
The reasonable answer may be matchups. A left-handed lineup could push Rodón up the board, while a series schedule might make a different order cleaner. Fine. The Yankees should use every edge they can find.
What they should not do is treat Rodón like the interchangeable third or fourth starter just because that was easier to say months ago. His work has made the pecking order less tidy. Good pitchers tend to do that.
The rotation debate is not settled, and it should not be. Rodón has made sure it will be an actual decision instead of a formality.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

With the postseason less than two weeks away, the Yankees are left holding their breath regarding the status of their slugging captain, Aaron Judge, who left Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins early with what the team described as right lower-leg tightness.
Judge, who started the game in right field, was seen wincing during his second and final at-bat of the afternoon in the top of the third inning following a check-swing. He was pinch-hit for by Heliot Ramos in the top of the sixth, sending up immediate red flags for a team fighting to catch the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the American League East.
Manager Aaron Boone said that Juge felt something in the first inning and took him out to make sure he didn’t “push through anything.”
He will undergo treatment, and the team will get a better sense of how severe the issue is on Thursday.
There may be some relief in that it is not his rib or oblique that is bothering him, though such a statement is a bit premature, considering the specifics of this lower-leg issue is unknown. Judge has already missed three months this season due to a rib injury that kept him out from late May to Sept. 7.
Wednesday’s game was just his seventh game back from the injured list, and he has struggled mightily after the long layoff, going 4-for-23 (.173) with one home run, three RBI, and 13 strikeouts.
Boone previously stated that he was going to take things slow with Judge because they forewent a rehab assignment. But he played six straight games before getting Tuesday off — the day after New York clinched its ninth postseason berth in 10 years.
The prospect of being without Judge this postseason should be a daunting one for the Yankees. Their offense struggled mightily without him, scoring 341 runs in the 84 games without him (4.06 runs per game). Only the Cincinnati Reds, Toronto Blue Jays, Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Angels, and Seattle Mariners scored fewer runs in all of baseball during that stretch.
Still, the Bronx Bombers should like their chances regardless of the status of their captain. The American League is exceptionally poor this season, with only six teams possessing records over .500. Three of them, including the Yankees, inhabit the AL East.
They also have one of the most imposing pitching staffs in all of baseball, as they are set to trot out AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodon in a shortened postseason rotation.

-
- As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns.
- Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question.
Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in between. And questions linger over the postseason availability of several other MLB difference-makers as October approaches.
Here is a look at the injury status and hopeful returns of impact players on playoff qualifiers and contenders:
American League East
Tampa Bay Rays: Acquired from Baltimore at the trade deadline, swingman Tyler Wells posted a 1.50 earned-run average before right forearm tightness sidelined him. He is back solely pitching from the bullpen, and could be a key piece for the Rays in their surprising surge to the division title.
Hopeful return: Slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls is recovering from a right hip flexor strain and signs point to him returning by October.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
New York Yankees: The return of staff ace Fried is huge for a team that has clinched a wild-card berth and remains a long step behind the Rays for a division title and first-round bye. The left-hander out of Studio City Harvard-Westlake High gave up one run while walking none over seven innings in his longest start in almost five months. Fried has had two arduous IL stints dealing with a bone bruise on his left elbow.
Hopeful returns: Giancarlo Stanton or Trent Grisham returning in October would give the Yankees lineup additional pop. Three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge has been back for a week since missing more than three months with a fractured rib.
Boston Red Sox: A right quadriceps strain has kept All-Star center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela sidelined for two weeks. However, Rafaela told NESN that he expects to be activated this weekend, a substantial addition to a team that likely will play the Yankees in wild-card series.
Hopeful return: A year ago, Garrett Crochet was 18-5 and led the AL with 205 1/3 innings pitched. This year, left shoulder inflammation and a lat strain have kept him sidelined since April. However, he has ramped up bullpen sessions and is targeting a postseason return as a reliever.
American League Central
Chicago White Sox: The most improved team in baseball is desperately trying to hold off the Guardians and win a division title after finishing last two years in a row. Chicago has enjoyed good health and added journeyman outfielder Tommy Pham from the Phillies on Aug. 31. Pham was activated from the IL on Wednesday and could provide valuable postseason experience to complement his young new teammates — he has hit .315 in 37 career playoff games.
Hopeful return: Drew Thorpe was reinstated from the 60-day IL on Wednesday and is an intriguing option. The right-hander from Cal Poly SLO was a key piece in the 2024 trade that sent Dylan Cease to the Padres but has spent nearly two full seasons on the shelf. Now healthy, his inclusion on the playoff roster would be a gamble that his elite stuff can mask his inexperience.
Cleveland Guardians: Jo Adell didn’t come off the IL, but the addition of the former confounding Angels prospect in an August salary dump has bolstered the Guardians’ outfield — long a problem area. Adell has driven in 28 runs in 38 games with Cleveland and joins glittering rookie Chase DeLauter and steady veteran Steven Kwan in a productive outfield.
Hopeful return: Reliever Shawn Armstrong, who signed a one-year, $5.5-million contract last offseason, has been sidelined since July 24 with a calf strain. Barring a setback in his final minor league rehab appearance, he could be activated in time for the playoffs.
American League West
Houston Astros: Correa, whose second act with Houston has been a flop because of injuries, was working on an accelerated comeback from May ankle surgery. A few days ago, team officials expressed optimism, but Tuesday they decided to shelve their shortstop when the ankle became inflamed after a workout. Houston is clinging to a one-game lead over the Texas Rangers in the AL West.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note.
Texas Rangers: Still in contention despite spending much of the season under .500, the Rangers welcomed back pitcher Nathan Eovaldi and third baseman Josh Jung from the injured list over the weekend. A calf strain had kept Jung sidelined since July 21 and Eovaldi had been out since Aug. 7 with elbow inflammation. Eovaldi, who has started in all but 20 of his 339 MLB appearances, will pitch out of the bullpen.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note.
National League East
Atlanta Braves: Reynaldo López inflated hopes of a late-career surge when he posted a 1.99 ERA over 25 starts in his first season with Atlanta. But injuries — including right shoulder inflammation this season — have severely limited his contribution. López was placed on the IL again Tuesday.
Hopeful return: Bryce Elder had an arthroscopic procedure to clean up bone fragments in his right knee on Sept. 8. The hope is that the right-handed starter can recover quickly enough to be counted upon in the postseason.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.
Philadelphia Phillies: Although an MRI found no structural damage to the throwing shoulder of stalwart starter Jesús Luzardo, the left-hander remains a question for the playoffs. He was placed on the 15-day IL retroactive to Sept. 12, and it is doubtful he could pitch again in the regular season. Luzardo has a 2.87 ERA across 29 starts this season.
Hopeful return: Tanner Banks, a major contributor to the Philadelphia bullpen in 2025, was reinstated from the 60-day IL over the weekend. Although he wasn’t effective earlier this season, Banks is welcomed back because Phillies relievers have been poor against left-handed hitters.
National League Central
Milwaukee Brewers: Huntington Beach Marina High product Jake Bauers has suffered from shin splints almost all season, and the pain has kept him from playing the outfield lately. He can play first base, but that takes slugger Andrew Vaughn out of the lineup. Bauers, with 26 home runs and 83 RBIs, has been a key bat for Milwaukee. He has been particularly tough against the Dodgers, batting .348 with a .483 on-base percentage.
Hopeful return: Brandon Woodruff, one of the best starters in baseball when healthy, is rehabbing from shoulder inflammation that sidelined him in July. The Brewers are nearly guaranteed a first-round bye, giving Woodruff an extra week to build stamina.
Chicago Cubs: Shortstop and team leader Dansby Swanson will be welcomed back after missing a month with a left oblique injury. He is expected to rejoin the Cubs during their weekend series against the Cincinnati Reds.
Hopeful return: Left-handed starter Justin Steele is progressing through bullpen sessions and is almost ready to take the mound after missing the entire season with a left elbow flexor strain. Steele, whose record was 16-5 in 2023, likely would pitch from the bullpen in the postseason.
National League West
Dodgers: The loss of center fielder Andy Pages is significant. He can bat near the top or bottom of the order, displays power and speed, and had improved his patience at the plate enough to earn a career-high 45 walks in 128 games.
Hopeful return: Getting Ohtani healthy enough to produce at the plate is a priority, and his absence from the mound shouldn’t be felt if Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow pitch to their capabilities. Meanwhile, Edwin Diaz might not even make the playoff roster.
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
San Diego Padres: While recovering from Tommy John surgery, starter Joe Musgrove made it a goal to be ready for the postseason. Recovery difficulties between starts have made his status doubtful, however. Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, has pitched well in two starts since coming off the IL and appears ready.
Hopeful return: Ramón Laureano, a 2025 trade deadline acquisition with a potent bat, last played May 30 because of hip inflammation. However, he told reporters that the chances of him playing in the postseason are “less than 5%.”
Arizona Diamondbacks: Zac Gallen was activated from the 60-day IL and Michael Soroka from the 15-day IL, giving the Diamondbacks two starters in their push to win a wild-card berth. Gallen, a proven starter who has been horrendous in 2026, has been out since the All-Star break with elbow inflammation. Soroka was out only two weeks with the same ailment.
Hopeful return: Third baseman Nolan Arenado suffered an injury to his left thumb Tuesday, the same injury he sustained in late August. It’s doubtful the injury would sideline the 14-year veteran with games this week being so important, yet the Diamondbacks have to hope the injury doesn’t impact his productivity.

Yankees RHP Clarke Schmidt Returns As Reliever After 14-Month Rehab
The New York Yankees returned right-handed pitcher Clarke Schmidt from his rehabilitation assignment and reinstated him from the injured list on Wednesday, aiming to integrate the 30-year-old into their bullpen for the postseason following his 14-month recovery from elbow surgery.
Schmidt had an internal brace procedure on his ulnar collateral ligament on July 11, 2025, and began minor league rehab on Aug. 29. The 2017 first-round draft pick was used exclusively as a starter since 2023, but with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and Gerrit Cole in the rotation, Schmidt will transition to relief.
"It's been a long journey, a lot of work that goes into this. A lot of long days, early mornings," Schmidt said before the game Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins. "I've just been itching to come back."
The Yankees designated popular multi-position player Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster for Schmidt. Cabrera missed most of the 2025 season with a severe ankle injury.
"I’m blessed to have a lot of guys on this team that you just admire and respect and love doing the job with on a daily basis," manager Aaron Boone said. "Oswaldo’s right there at the top of that list."
Reporting by The Associated Press.

It's been a nice start to the week in the Yankees' home-away-from-home. On Monday night, they clinched a postseason berth with a 7-3 win against the Twins. On Tuesday evening, they fielded the proverbial "hangover lineup" of sorts and still cruised to an 8-1 victory behind a strong start from Max Fried and plenty of strong performances at the plate.
On today's getaway day game in Minneapolis, Carlos Rodón leads the Yankees' effort for a sweep. His most recent start against the Mets was perhaps the best of his season, as he held down the crosstown rivals for one run in 6.1 innings—with eight strikeouts to just one walk. For Rodón, who has for various reasons not pitched deep into games as routinely as he did in 2025, a second straight start of six or more innings would be an excellent sign as he prepares for the postseason.
The Twins, now 4-9 in September, will look to young righty Zebby Matthews, who has turned in an uneven campaign on the hill this season. His past three starts have been illustrative of the step-forward-step-back tendency which has tormented many a young hurler. On August 30th, he twirled an absolute gem, pitching into the ninth inning against the rival White Sox with just one run allowed in a win. His next appearance, also against Chicago, was a far more pedestrian five-inning, four-run effort. Then last time out, he failed to escape the third inning in Detroit—walking four batters and surrendering five runs to hit the showers early.
While the Yankees rested a few of their starters for last night's contest, including Aaron Judge, it didn't prevent them from running up the score. Today, Judge returns to the lineup card, hitting third behind DH Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, who led the way with three hits and a homer last night. Cleanup hitter Luis García Jr., Spencer Jones, and George Lombard Jr. will make up the middle of the order, with Ryan McMahon, Austin Wells, and second baseman Anthony Volpe (it's still weird to say that) pulling up the rear.

The Yankees’ pitching picture continues to regain its health, as Clarke Schmidt was reinstated from the 60-day injured list on Wednesday as he returns from Tommy John surgery.
The 30-year-old right-hander had been out since July 3 of last season when he was diagnosed with a torn UCL that not only required Tommy John surgery, but also an internal brace procedure. He had a 3.32 ERA and a 1.090 WHIP in 14 starts last season before the injury
He should be in play for a full-time spot in the rotation next season. Over 30 starts between the 2024 and 2025 seasons, he sported a 3.07 ERA and a 1.140 WHIP, which would make an already-great starting five that much more elite.
In the immediate future, though, Schmidt will likely spend this upcoming postseason in the bullpen. Shortened rotations would likely see the Yankees roll with four starters, and there is no usurping Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, or Carlos Rodon.
To make room for him on the 40-man roster, the Yankees designated utilityman Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment. He played just three games with the big-league club this season, spending most of his time with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. The 27-year-old was slashing .288/.345/.444 in 122 games, but owned a .635 career OPS across parts of five seasons with the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Durante casi toda la última década, a Gerrit Cole le tocaban automáticamente los partidos más importantes de los Yankees.
Esa seguridad se ha esfumado.
A menos de dos semanas de que termine octubre, el lanzador que marcaba la diferencia en el equipo se ha convertido en su mayor incógnita. La velocidad sigue ahí, pero los resultados se han deteriorado en el peor momento posible. Aaron Boone ha intentado restarle importancia a la preocupación. Pero lo que pasa sigue haciendo que eso sea cada vez más difícil.
Cole, ganador del Premio Cy Young de los Yankees en 2023, ha encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, la cifra más alta en cualquier racha de dos salidas de su carrera, según MLB.com. El que antes era una apuesta segura para el primer partido ha bajado puestos en la jerarquía de octubre y ha generado un auténtico debate sobre si debería ser el lanzador titular en un partido a vida o muerte.
Para un equipo de los Yankees que tiene el mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) del béisbol, esto es como una grieta en los cimientos. Nueva York se aseguró el lunes su plaza en los playoffs y ahora tiene un balance de 88-63. El pitcheo es la razón por la que el club cree que puede llegar lejos. Se suponía que Cole iba a ser el pilar de esa fortaleza, no que se convirtiera en su mayor incertidumbre.
Un problema mental que aterroriza a los Yankees
El 6 de septiembre, Cole encajó jonrones de los tres primeros bateadores de los Padres a los que se enfrentó. Fernando Tatis Jr., Jake Cronenworth y Manny Machado conectaron tres jonrones seguidos.
Seis días después, los Mets le dieron una paliza al as de los Yankees en una goleada por 12-2. Francisco Lindor conectó un jonrón con el tercer lanzamiento de Cole. Más tarde, el novato Carson Benge también le mandó la pelota fuera del campo con un slider. Cole aguantó 4 1/3 entradas, encajó cinco carreras y tres jonrones, y se llevó abucheos al salir del campo.
Tras el partido, su explicación hizo que la derrota de los Yankees pareciera aún peor.
Cole tiene una efectividad de 6,08 en sus últimas cuatro salidas, con 17 ponches en 22 2/3 entradas, y ha encajado al menos tres carreras limpias en cuatro partidos seguidos.
En lo que va de temporada, tiene un balance de 8-9, con una efectividad de 3,67 y 20 jonrones permitidos en 115 1/3 entradas. Los Yankees solo han promediado 3,67 carreras en sus salidas, lo que ha convertido partidos que antes parecían pan comido en auténticas loterías.
Lo que realmente preocupa a los Yankees
La preocupación no es que Cole haya perdido de repente su nivel de Grandes Ligas. Es por qué los bateadores se ven tan cómodos frente a él.
Los analistas de YES Network, David Cone y Paul O’Neill, plantearon la posibilidad de que Cole esté delatando sus lanzamientos, lo que podría explicar por qué los bateadores han sabido manejar una bola rápida que sigue alcanzando las 98 mph.
El entrenador de lanzadores, Matt Blake, no lo descartó.
«Es posible», dijo Blake, y añadió que «esa es una de las cosas que vamos a analizar».
Blake también señaló un problema más sencillo. Cole está lanzando strikes a un ritmo sin precedentes en su carrera, pero demasiados se quedan en el centro del strike zone.
«Tenemos que sacar la bola de la parte más ancha del plato», dijo Blake. «Además, quizá tengamos que mejorar la ejecución con dos strikes para lanzar a mejores zonas».
Cole ha reconocido el problema sin pretender haberlo resuelto.
«Hay que empezar a hacer ajustes», dijo Cole.
También rechazó la teoría de que delata sus lanzamientos, diciendo que sus lanzamientos deberían seguir dándonos margen incluso si los bateadores los anticipan.
«Aunque sepan (lo que viene), sigue siendo difícil de batear», dijo Cole. «Mis lanzamientos deberían darnos más margen de error».
Cómo está cambiando la rotación
La mala racha de Cole ha trastocado la jerarquía de la rotación.
Cam Schlittler, en una segunda temporada espectacular, se ha revelado como el mejor lanzador del equipo y un probable candidato al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Se perfila como el abridor del primer partido. Max Fried, que vuelve tras una lesión en el codo, y Carlos Rodón tienen ambos un promedio de carreras limpias por debajo de 3,00 y parecen opciones más seguras para los primeros partidos de la serie.
El enfrentamiento complica aún más las cosas. Es probable que los Yankees se enfrenten a Boston en una serie de comodín al mejor de tres. Cole tiene una efectividad de 5,30 en su carrera contra los Red Sox, y solo los Mets le han bateado con más fuerza.
El veterano columnista Joel Sherman resumió la cuestión de octubre en una sola palabra: «correa». Según su hipótesis, Cole empezaría un partido de mitad de temporada con mucho menos margen de error.
«Creo que Schlittler, Fried y Cole van a ser los titulares», dijo Sherman. «La diferencia es que a Cole le van a dar muy, muy poco margen, algo que, por lo general, no habría tenido».
Sherman también vinculó directamente el techo de los Yankees en la postemporada a que Cole y Aaron Judge recuperen su mejor forma.
«Los Yankees podrían quedarse fuera de los playoffs en menos de 48 horas o podrían ganar la Serie Mundial», dijo Sherman. «Ambas opciones están sobre la mesa y las posibilidades de éxito aumentan mucho más si Cole y Judge se ponen las pilas en las próximas dos semanas, porque son Gerrit Cole y Aaron Judge, y son grandes jugadores cuando están en forma».
Los datos sobre los lanzamientos con efecto explican el colapso
Cole ha mantenido a los bateadores zurdos en un OPS de 0,683. El problema son los bateadores diestros, que tienen un slugging de 0,448 contra él, la cifra más alta que han registrado los diestros en cualquier temporada de su carrera.
Las bolas con efecto del as de los Yankees son las que están causando más daño. Los bateadores diestros tienen un promedio de slugging de 0,652 contra su curva, con diferencia la peor cifra de su carrera. Tienen un promedio de slugging de 0,463 contra su slider, también un récord personal y, con holgada diferencia, su peor marca como jugador de los Yankees.
Además, esos lanzamientos están fallando menos. Su curva solo ha generado un 17 % de fallos contra los bateadores diestros, mientras que su slider se sitúa en el 25 %. Además, está lanzando el slider en el centro de la zona contra los bateadores diestros con la mayor frecuencia de su carrera, lo que explica tanto la reducción de los fallos como los contactos más fuertes.
Los modelos de calidad de los lanzamientos muestran el mismo deterioro. El slider de Cole ha bajado de una puntuación de 125 en Stuff+ en 2020 a 106 esta temporada. La curva de la estrella de los Yankees ha bajado de 120 a 104. Ambas siguen estando por encima de la media, pero el margen que antes le hacía imparable se ha reducido.
Cole cumplió 36 años el 8 de septiembre y está en su primera temporada tras recuperarse de una operación de Tommy John, un año que, según la medicina deportiva, suele ser menos brillante que el segundo. Ya sea por un problema mecánico, por delatar sus lanzamientos o por simple cansancio, Nueva York tiene menos de dos semanas para encontrar la respuesta.
Por ahora, el as que en su día se encargaba de las tareas más importantes está haciendo una prueba para un papel en octubre que antes dominaba.

BRONX, N.Y. — Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen a 3 1/2 partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Pero una de las decisiones más importantes que ha tomado la organización este mes de septiembre no tiene nada que ver con la alineación de Aaron Boone ni con los planes de pitcheo para octubre.
Esto ha dado lugar a seis despidos en lo que va de septiembre.
Todo esto está pasando a miles de millas del Yankee Stadium, en la República Dominicana, Venezuela y otros mercados donde se descubre a los futuros Yankees años antes de que la mayoría de los aficionados sepan siquiera sus nombres.
De esa cantera salieron Robinson Canó, Alfonso Soriano, Gary Sánchez e Iván Nova. Los Yankees siguieron invirtiendo ahí a medida que cambiaban las normas sobre bonificaciones, la tecnología y los métodos de evaluación de jugadores amateurs.
La presión sobre esa área lleva meses aumentando. Donny Rowland, director de ojeadores internacionales desde hacía mucho tiempo, no renovó su contrato cuando este expiró en noviembre. Los Yankees ascendieron entonces a Mario Garza, que llevaba 16 años en la organización y tenía experiencia en el desarrollo de jugadores, las operaciones en Latinoamérica y el desarrollo del béisbol, para que se encargara de los ojeadores internacionales en enero.
La transición tuvo un coste inmediato. Wandy Asigen, uno de los mejores jugadores de la promoción internacional de 2026, se echó atrás en el acuerdo que tenía previsto con los Yankees tras la marcha de Rowland y fichó por los Mets por 3,9 millones de dólares. Nueva York también empezó el periodo de fichajes con un fondo de 5,44 millones de dólares, el más bajo de la MLB (empatado con otro equipo) tras perder un millón de dólares por fichar a Max Fried.
Cuando Garza se hizo cargo, Brian Cashman describió algo que iba más allá de un simple cambio de personal.
«Es un gran evaluador de talento», dijo Cashman. «Conoce nuestros sistemas. Ya sabe todo el personal que queremos tener. Quieres evaluación, quieres que todo esté conectado con la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos. Eso le dará ventaja a la hora de relanzar ese departamento y seguir adelante».
Esas declaraciones públicas cobran ahora importancia porque dejaron claro, meses antes de septiembre, que Nueva York veía el departamento como algo que había que reconstruir, en lugar de simplemente mantener.
El relanzamiento se ha convertido en una reestructuración más amplia de los Yankees
Ese relanzamiento se ha acelerado.
Cinco empleados del departamento de ojeadores internacionales de los Yankees no han sido renovados en lo que el periodista Francys Romero ha descrito como una «primera oleada». Se trata de los ojeadores de la zona de la República Dominicana José Sabino y Arturo Peña Jr., el ojeador de la zona de Santo Domingo Moisés Brito, el asistente de vídeo Miguel Mojica y el supervisor de Venezuela José Gavidia.
Romero describió los cambios como parte de un plan más amplio.
«Los Yankees tienen previsto reestructurar su departamento de ojeadores internacionales y, según fuentes del sector, ya han despedido a cinco personas en los últimos días. Entre los ojeadores que no seguirán están José Sabino y Arturo Peña Jr. (ojeador de la zona de Cibao, República Dominicana), Moisés Brito (ojeador de la zona de Santo Domingo), Miguel Mojica (asistente de vídeo) y José Gavidia (supervisor de Venezuela)».
Estas medidas se produjeron tras la salida del veterano ojeador Víctor Mata, cuya trayectoria en los Yankees se prolongó durante más de tres décadas. Mata ayudó a evaluar o fichar a Canó, Sánchez, Soriano, Nova y Zoilo Almonte.
La naturaleza exacta de la salida de Mata sigue siendo objeto de debate. Romero informó de que los Yankees lo dejaron marchar. El periodista Mike Rodríguez ofreció una versión diferente, afirmando que Mata se retiró y recibió las prestaciones asociadas a su larga trayectoria en el equipo. Los Yankees no han dado públicamente una explicación detallada.
La cronología apunta a un reinicio planificado
La racha es más larga que los movimientos de esta semana.
A Rowland no le renovaron el contrato en noviembre. Garza fue nombrado en enero y Cashman utilizó públicamente la palabra «relanzamiento». Los Yankees funcionaron entonces toda la temporada bajo un nuevo liderazgo antes de la marcha de Mata y los cinco cambios adicionales en la plantilla que se produjeron en septiembre.
Esto apunta más bien a un reajuste estructural que a una reacción ante un solo prospecto o una sola promoción de fichajes.
Había motivos para replantearse los resultados. Un análisis de FanGraphs sobre el sistema de cantera de los Yankees, publicado en marzo, señalaba que el club solía destinar una gran parte de su fondo de bonificaciones internacionales a uno o dos jugadores caros y que demasiadas de esas apuestas millonarias no habían dado los frutos esperados.
En ese mismo informe se decía que el sistema necesitaba más talento entre los jugadores de campo tras las últimas salidas por graduación. Eso no aclara por qué se despidió a ningún ojeador, pero ayuda a entender por qué los Yankees se replantearían cómo identifican, valoran y forman a los jugadores internacionales.
La marcha de Asigen hizo que el tema cobrara más relevancia. Este campocorto de 16 años estaba considerado uno de los mejores jugadores de su generación y se esperaba que firmara con los Yankees, pero cambió de planes tras la salida de Rowland.
Ahora los comentarios que hizo Cashman en enero parecen más importantes
La pista más clara sobre qué hay detrás de la reorganización de los Yankees podría haber llegado ocho meses antes de los últimos cambios.
La descripción que hizo Cashman de Garza hacía hincapié en la colaboración entre la evaluación, la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos. El currículum de Garza une todas esas áreas. Antes de este puesto, fue director de desarrollo de béisbol en 2024 y 2025, y anteriormente trabajó en operaciones en Latinoamérica y en el desarrollo de jugadores internacionales.
Esto hace que los cambios parezcan menos un rechazo al ojeo tradicional y más un intento de cambiar cómo circula la información de ojeo por la organización.
El ojeo internacional sigue dependiendo de las relaciones, la evaluación presencial y el conocimiento local. La carrera de Mata puso de manifiesto ese valor. Pero ahora los Yankees están colocando al frente del departamento a un líder con experiencia reciente en desarrollo y sistemas.
La apuesta es importante. Nueva York está dejando atrás a miembros del equipo con profundas raíces en Latinoamérica, al tiempo que pide a un nuevo grupo que mantenga esas relaciones y modernice la evaluación al mismo tiempo.
El veredicto tardará años en salir
No hay resultados inmediatos que reflejen una reforma en el sistema de ojeadores internacionales.
Un cambio en la alineación se puede valorar esa misma noche. Pero una decisión que afecte a un joven promesa de 16 años puede que no dé frutos en las Grandes Ligas hasta dentro de cinco o seis años.
Eso es lo que hace que el momento sea tan significativo. Los Yankees tienen un balance de 88-63, se han asegurado un puesto en octubre y ocupan la primera plaza de comodín de la Liga Americana. Sin embargo, estos cambios están pensados para las plantillas mucho más allá de la actual carrera por los playoffs.
La cronología que se conoce está clara: Rowland se va, ascienden a Garza, se pierde a uno de los mejores fichajes, Mata se marcha y no se renueva a otros cinco miembros del personal internacional. Lo que los Yankees no han dicho públicamente es si habrá más cambios.
Por ahora, las declaraciones de Cashman en enero son las que ofrecen una explicación más clara. Los Yankees querían relanzar el departamento y vincular más estrechamente el trabajo de ojeadores con la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos.
Ocho meses después, ese relanzamiento está cambiando el perfil de las personas que decidirán qué jóvenes jugadores entrarán próximamente en el sistema de los Yankees.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

Yankees receive great Clarke Schmidt news amid Twins series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees already have a strong pitching staff.
Now, they'll be adding another veteran arm with less than two weeks remaining in the regular season.
On Tuesday, Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News reported that right-hander Clarke Schmidt will return from the 60-day injured list on Wednesday.
Schmidt, 30, underwent Tommy John Surgery last July and recently completed a rehab assignment.
He made five appearances between Double-A and Triple-A, throwing one to two innings at a time. According to Anthony Franco of MLB Trade Rumors, Schmidt averaged 94.1 mph on his fastball.
In all likelihood, Schmidt will be an option out of manager Aaron Boone's bullpen, not in the rotation.
New York's rotation already has a more than solid top five of Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon, and Will Warren.
Schmidt made 14 starts in 2025 before learning surgery was required. He posted a 3.32 ERA and allowed a career-low 6.4 hits per nine innings.
To open space on the active roster, right-hander Bradley Hanner was optioned to Triple-A by the Yankees.

Por The Associated Press
Agencia de noticias
Minneapolis - Max Fried consiguió su primera victoria desde el 27 de abril, respaldado por jonrones de Cody Bellinger y Spencer Jones que ayudaron a los Yankees de Nueva York a mantenerse en la pelea por el Este de la Liga Americana con un triunfo el martes 8-1 sobre los Twins de Minnesota.
Fried (5-4) permitió una carrera en siete sólidas entradas y 88 lanzamientos, en su apertura más duradera en casi cinco meses, para asegurar que los Yankees (88-63) se mantuvieran a 3.5 juegos de Tampa Bay (91-59) en la lucha por el liderato divisional.
Los Yankees, que aseguraron al menos un puesto de comodín el lunes, necesitarán que Fried mantenga este nivel en la postemporada.
Fried, quien pasó 71 juegos en la lista de lesionados en dos periodos por una contusión ósea en el codo, tiene una efectividad de 1.83 con 50 ponches en 44.1 entradas en nueve aperturas después del receso del Juego de Estrellas.
Bellinger, que conectó tres hits y recibió una base por bolas, puso en marcha rápidamente a los Yankees con su decimosexto cuadrangular, un batazo de dos carreras después de que Ben Rice abrió el juego con un sencillo ante Bailey Ober (7-6). Bellinger batea para .377 (26 de 69) en sus últimos 17 juegos.
Jones conectó su décimo jonrón con dos salidas en la sexta, un cuadrangular de tres carreras ante Taylor Rogers. Un error defensivo del campocorto novato Kaelen Culpepper hizo que las cuatro carreras del episodio fueran sucias.
Nueva York tiene 11 jugadores con 10 o más jonrones esta temporada.
La estrella del jardín derecho Aaron Judge, que busca recuperar su forma tras regresar recientemente de una costilla rota, se quedó en la banca para descansar mientras los Yankees acumulaban 14 hits.

When the champagne celebration ended Monday night, after the Yankees removed their goggles and the booze-filled plastic coverings protecting the visitors’ clubhouse at Target Field were taken down, some of their postseason certainties were starting to take shape.
They, after the Blue Jays lost, had clinched a spot in the tournament. Barring a collapse by the Rays over the final two weeks, the Yankees will start from a wild-card position. Barring a collapse by their own roster, they’ll occupy the top wild-card spot. And barring any last-minute nightmares, Aaron Judge, with his home run Monday as evidence, Max Fried, who’s trying to rediscover his vintage form (as he did in Tuesday’s 8-1 win over the Twins), Gerrit Cole, who’s trying to figure out why he’s letting up all these home runs and Cam Schlittler, in the midst of strengthening his case for the American League Cy Young Award, are all healthy.
But in a year where the Yankees kept needing to navigate injuries, where star after star after star kept missing time, unlikely heroes materialized. And if this group ends up being the one to snap the World Series title drought that dates back to 2009, those names — from Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn to second-half Austin Wells and José Caballero — will need to contribute.
Every contender has its stars. The Judges. The Coles. The Schlittlers, as well as the Frieds, the Ben Rices, the David Bednars and the Cody Bellingers. The constants expected to anchor the run. The faces who’ve been on that October stage before.

MINNESOTA — Impeded by multiple bone bruises in his prized left elbow, Max Fried recorded his first win since April 27 on Tuesday night when the Yankees beat the Twins, 8-1.
The southpaw also completed seven innings for the first time since April 22 while holding Minnesota to one earned run, which came on an Emmanuel Rodriguez single in the second inning. Fried struck out six, and he didn’t allow any walks over 88 pitches after a couple of free passes and long at-bats limited him to just 3.1 innings his last time out on Sept. 10.
“I thought he threw really well. He had a little of everything going. He did a good job with the shape of his breaking balls,” Aaron Boone said. “I like where he’s at after that.”
“It definitely was nice to be able to put what felt like a full start together,” added Fried, who is now four outings removed from his most recent stint on the injured list.
While Fried has a 2.63 ERA, it’s been a bumpy and achy year for the co-ace. His bone bruises have limited him to just 19 starts, making consistency and length harder to come by.
However, Fried believes he is close to being fully built up — he said he was only supposed to throw 80-85 pitches on Tuesday — and he now has reason to be encouraged with less than two weeks remaining in the regular season and the playoffs approaching.
“It’s really nice,” Fried said. “You want to be able to be throwing well at this time of the year, and I’m just really thankful to the medical staff, coaches, everyone that’s kind of been [watching] my health and getting me to this point to be in a position to succeed.”
Fried did note that he still wants to be sharper as he puts the finishing touches on his injury-riddled season, though. One pitch to watch in that regard is his four-seam fastball, which he only threw 10 times on Tuesday with a 93.7-mph average velocity. That was down 1.2 mph from Fried’s season average.
His heater’s velocity has fluctuated this year, and his bone bruises were most uncomfortable when he was extending at full force. Fortunately for Fried, he has a seven-pitch mix to work with.
With Fried fresh off a night in which he made good use of that mix, he already had his sights set on his next start, which will come against the first-place Rays next week in New York.
With the second-place Yankees, down 3.5 games, trying to overcome the odds and win the American League East, they will need Fried at his best against Tampa. He’s looking forward to the opportunity.
“It’s going to be playoff baseball,” he said.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Durante dos noches seguidas, los Yankees han sumado siete carreras con el mismo golpe. Aaron Judge conectó un jonrón de tres carreras el lunes. Veinticuatro horas después, Spencer Jones lo repitió ante un rival del que Nueva York intentó protegerlo en su momento.
Jones conectó un lanzamiento «sweeper» 2-2 del zurdo de los Twins, Taylor Rogers, en la sexta entrada del martes y lo mandó a 423 pies, justo al centro del campo. Ese jonrón de tres carreras dio a los Yankees una ventaja de 7-1 en lo que acabó siendo una victoria por 8-1 en el Target Field.
El enfrentamiento hizo que el swing resultara más revelador que la distancia. Rogers se había enfrentado a 133 bateadores zurdos esta temporada sin permitir ningún jonrón antes de que el novato de los Yankees rompiera esa racha. Jones había fallado una serie de lanzamientos rasantes antes de conectar otro por el centro y mandarlo fuera a 108 mph.
Cody Bellinger ya había dado a los Yankees una ventaja de 2-0 en la primera entrada con su decimosexto jonrón, mientras que Max Fried lanzó siete entradas cediendo solo una carrera. Los Yankees terminaron con 14 hits —todos los titulares consiguieron al menos uno—, mejoraron su balance a 88-63 y ganaron por séptima vez en ocho partidos.
El jonrón de Jones fue el décimo, lo que le convierte en el undécimo jugador de los Yankees en alcanzar las dos cifras esta temporada, la cifra más alta del club desde 2019.
Su poder había estado un poco apagado durante casi dos semanas, pero su bate no. Jones bateó .333 durante esa racha de 11 partidos sin jonrones. En sus últimos 25 partidos, ha conectado 28 de 81, con un promedio de .346, 10 hits de más de una base, cinco jonrones, 19 carreras impulsadas, 17 carreras anotadas y un OPS de .993.
Cada vez es más difícil pasar por alto la curva de crecimiento
Las estadísticas de Jones esta temporada, .259/.331/.452, no reflejan lo mucho que ha cambiado su perfil en los Yankees. Empezó mayo con un promedio de .167/.259/.167 en 10 partidos, subió a .255/.340/.468 en junio y alcanzó un slugging de .611 en ocho partidos de julio. En agosto registró unas estadísticas de .239/.290/.446, pero en septiembre ha logrado un .340/.415/.532 en 13 partidos.
La tendencia general de la segunda mitad de la temporada es parecida. El novato de los Yankees ha bateado .271/.337/.490 desde el parón del All-Star, tras registrar .233/.317/.370 antes de él. Lo ha conseguido mientras jugaba habitualmente en el centro del campo y seguía trabajando para superar los problemas con los strikeouts que le han perseguido desde las ligas menores.
El exentrenador de los Yankees, Joe Girardi, destacó el alcance de esa mejora antes del partido del lunes. Girardi señaló los ajustes de Jones con corredores en posición de anotar, su capacidad para atrapar lanzamientos a gran velocidad, su defensa, su velocidad en las bases y la potencia de su brazo.
«Es capaz de hacerlo todo», dijo Girardi.
Bellinger, que comparte el jardín de los Yankees con Jones, dijo que el cambio va más allá de los resultados. Destacó lo tranquilo que se ve el novato, independientemente de quién esté lanzando.
«Ha sido increíble. Es decir, su swing es… es un swing realmente bueno, y mentalmente entiende lo que quiere hacer contra [los zurdos] y sabe lo que tiene que hacer frente a ellos», dijo Bellinger. «Da igual si el lanzador es diestro o zurdo, no parece que le afecte. Tiene un buen enfoque».
Jones le ha dado la vuelta al tema de los turnos
Las cifras explican por qué la estrategia inicial de los Yankees ya no encaja. Jones ha tenido 51 turnos al bate contra lanzadores zurdos y batea con un promedio de .435, un porcentaje de embasado de .490 y un porcentaje de slugging de .761, lo que le da un OPS de 1,251. Tiene 20 hits en 46 turnos al bate, incluyendo tres jonrones y 12 carreras impulsadas.
Entre los bateadores de la MLB con al menos 50 turnos al bate contra lanzadores zurdos, tanto su promedio de bateo como su OPS ocupan el primer puesto. Es algo inusual para un novato de los Yankees que llegó a las Grandes Ligas con dudas sobre su capacidad para evitar los strikes y al que, al principio, se le dosificaba con cuidado en los enfrentamientos contra lanzadores del mismo lado.
Además, los enfrentamientos contra lanzadores diestros representan una parte desproporcionada de su rendimiento. Jones suma 59 hits, 10 jonrones y 37 carreras impulsadas en un total de 78 partidos. Según un cálculo de PinstripesNation, solo alrededor del 20 % de sus turnos al bate han sido contra lanzadores zurdos, pero esos enfrentamientos suponen aproximadamente el 34 % de sus hits, el 30 % de sus jonrones y el 32 % de sus carreras impulsadas.
En sus últimos 32 turnos al bate, el jardinero de los Yankees tiene un promedio de bateo de .317, un OPS de .900, un porcentaje de slugging de .532 y cinco jonrones. Los Yankees también estaban pendientes de si la calidad de sus turnos al bate se mantenía incluso cuando el swing de jonrón desaparecía temporalmente.
Esas cifras han cambiado la forma en que el entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, lo maneja. A principios de temporada, Boone intentó facilitar la adaptación del novato zurdo a la vida en las Grandes Ligas limitando su exposición frente a lanzadores zurdos. Más de cuatro meses después, esa protección ha desaparecido prácticamente por completo.
«Le estaba ayudando a adaptarse poco a poco. Y la verdad es que ha irrumpido con fuerza», dijo Boone con una risita. «Además, se ha enfrentado a muchos lanzadores zurdos difíciles y, la verdad, creo que ha sabido controlar sus turnos al bate, lo cual es genial de ver».
Puede que la duda sobre la alineación de octubre ya se esté resolviendo sola
Antes, los Yankees tenían una razón muy clara para proteger a Jones de los zurdos. Ahora ya no. Su rendimiento contra los zurdos se ha convertido en uno de sus puntos fuertes, lo que elimina la razón basada en el emparejamiento para dejarlo en el banquillo cuando, en octubre, los bullpens empiezan a recurrir a especialistas.
Esto es importante porque la situación en el centro del campo ha cambiado rápidamente. Trent Grisham ha bateado .211/.308/.395 en 121 partidos, mientras que Jones ha pasado de tener un papel esporádico en los Yankees a ser titular a medida que la lucha por los playoffs se va ajustando. Su capacidad para mantenerse en la alineación tanto contra lanzadores diestros como zurdos le da a Boone más libertad a la hora de manejar a Bellinger, Heliot Ramos y el resto de la plantilla.
Los Yankees aún tienen que decidir cómo encajan todas las piezas cuando la plantilla esté al completo. Jones ha simplificado mucho una parte de ese debate. Lo que en mayo era un punto débil que Boone intentó gestionar, ahora parece un enfrentamiento que los rivales tendrán que tener en cuenta en octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario abajo.

MINNEAPOLIS — Apenas se había secado el champán cuando los Yankees se enfrentaron a la pregunta que quedaba pendiente desde la noche anterior: ¿Aparecería sin energía un equipo que se había pasado la noche de fiesta hasta altas horas de la madrugada?
Pues no fue así.
Cody Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la primera entrada; los Yankees terminaron con 14 hits —cada titular consiguió al menos uno— y Nueva York nunca estuvo por detrás en el marcador en la victoria por 8-1 sobre los Twins en el Target Field el martes.
Pero la cifra que más importaba para los Yankees en octubre era el número de lanzamientos de Max Fried.
Tras una salida en la que le costó mucho completar 3 1/3 entradas contra Colorado, Fried lanzó siete entradas con 88 lanzamientos, cediendo una carrera y seis hits, con seis strikeouts y ninguna base por bolas. Fue su salida más larga desde el 22 de abril y su primera victoria desde el 27 de abril. En Colorado, el lanzador de los Yankees necesitó 80 lanzamientos para conseguir 10 outs. El martes, solo necesitó ocho más para lograr 21.
Fried dijo que un pequeño ajuste en el control de sus lanzamientos lentos lo cambió todo.
Cómo los Yankees sentenciaron el partido desde el principio
Después de que Dean Kremer les limitara a dos hits, los Yankees se lanzaron a por Bailey Ober. Ben Rice, tras estar a punto de recibir un pelotazo, abrió la entrada con un sencillo. Bellinger le siguió con su decimosexto jonrón al centro-derecha.
Bellinger conectó 3 de 4 con una base por bolas y lleva un promedio de bateo de 0,377 en sus últimos 17 partidos, con cinco jonrones desde que volvió tras una lesión en el tendón de la corva. El promedio del bateador de los Yankees subió a 0,272, su mejor marca desde el 22 de junio.
Anthony Volpe y Ali Sánchez conectaron dos sencillos seguidos en la segunda entrada, pero Ober dejó a ambos en base. Minnesota respondió cuando Royce Lewis llegó a base con un sencillo al cuadro, robó la segunda y anotó gracias a un sencillo impulsor de Emmanuel Rodríguez con dos outs. Fried zanjó la jugada con un pickoff de libro contra Rodríguez.
Los Yankees respondieron en la tercera entrada. Heliot Ramos consiguió una base por bolas, Luis García Jr. conectó un sencillo y George Lombard Jr. bateó un sencillo impulsador con dos outs por la banda derecha, poniendo el marcador 3-1 a su favor. Volpe consiguió otra base por bolas y llenó las bases, pero el batazo de Sánchez al centro se quedó en la zona de advertencia.
Ober repartió nueve hits a lo largo de 5 1/3 entradas y encajó tres carreras, mientras Nueva York dejaba a sus corredores en las bases una y otra vez. Eso cambió en la sexta.
Rice llegó a base por un error del campocorto Kaelen Culpepper, Bellinger consiguió una base por bolas tras cuatro lanzamientos y Ramos conectó un doble ante el zurdo Taylor Rogers para poner el 4-1 en el marcador.
Le tocó el turno a Spencer Jones. Tras fallar una serie de lanzamientos bajos y lentos, el bateador novato de los Yankees conectó el cuarto, que le llegó justo por el centro con una cuenta de 2-2, y lo mandó 423 pies al centro para un jonrón de tres carreras, poniendo el marcador 7-1.
Rogers no había cedido ningún jonrón a un bateador zurdo en toda la temporada, en 133 turnos al bate. Jones puso fin a esa racha. Ahora tiene un promedio de bateo de .435/.490/.761 contra lanzadores zurdos y se ha convertido en el undécimo Yankee con más de diez jonrones esta temporada, igualando el total del club en 2019.
Las cuatro carreras de la sexta entrada fueron sucias debido a un error de Culpepper.
Nueva York sumó una carrera en la novena entrada cuando Lombard consiguió una base por bolas, avanzó gracias a un roletazo de out y anotó gracias al sencillo de José Caballero ante Andrew Morris.
Todos los titulares de los Yankees consiguieron al menos un hit y llegaron a base. Ramos, Lombard y Volpe llegaron a base tres veces cada uno. Con esta victoria, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-63, tras encadenar siete victorias en ocho partidos y con una ventaja de seis partidos sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
El ajuste que hizo Fried entre sus salidas
Fried dijo que un mejor control de sus lanzamientos lentos le permitió utilizarlos en cualquier cuenta.
«Simplemente tuve más control sobre mis lanzamientos lentos. Pude lanzarlos para conseguir strikes. Siento que he podido lanzarlos en cualquier cuenta. Y tenía mucha, mucha confianza en eso. He trabajado muy bien con Ali (Sánchez) y, además, cuando tienes a la defensa haciendo grandes jugadas detrás de ti, eso te da más confianza», le dijo el as de los Yankees a Meredith Marakovits, de YES Network.
Era la novena salida de Fried desde que volvió tras su segunda baja por lesión, a causa de un hematoma óseo en el codo izquierdo. El objetivo de los Yankees era reducir el número de lanzamientos por entrada y que aguantara más tiempo en el montículo.
«La verdad es que me ha venido muy bien poder hacer lo que me ha parecido una salida completa, sin estar tan limitado por el recuento de lanzamientos», dijo Fried. «Aún así, llegué a los 88 lanzamientos y terminé la séptima entrada, así que me alegro de haber podido tachar eso de la lista. Pero es una mezcla de sentirme bien con dónde estamos y, al mismo tiempo, saber que todavía tenemos cosas en las que trabajar».
El entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, dijo que Fried podría mejorar aún más la próxima vez.
«Me gusta cómo está ahora, y espero que pueda seguir mejorando un poco más en el próximo partido y que siga así», dijo Boone. «Pero me ha encantado cómo ha atacado la zona de strike, cómo ha controlado los conteos y cómo ha tenido mucha presencia con la mayoría de sus lanzamientos esta noche».
¿Por qué es importante el momento en octubre?
La salud y la carga de trabajo de Fried son clave para las cuentas de los Yankees de cara a la postemporadahttps://pinstripesnation.com/mlb-2026-postseason-schedule-yankees-2026-08-11/. Tras el partido del martes, tenía una efectividad de 2,63 y, desde el parón del All-Star, acumula una efectividad de 1,83 con 50 strikeouts en 44 1/3 entradas en nueve partidos como titular.
Los datos sobre los lanzamientos coinciden. Según un gráfico de Pitch Profiler, Fried lanzó su «sweeper» 19 veces, lo que supone el 21,6 % de sus 88 lanzamientos. Los bateadores fallaron el golpe en el 70 % de las ocasiones y obtuvieron un promedio de embasado ponderado esperado de 0,098.
Su bola curva, lanzada 15 veces, generó un porcentaje de fallos del 33,3 %. El cambio de velocidad del as de los Yankees , lanzado 13 veces, generó un porcentaje de fallos del 37,5 % y un promedio esperado de .175.
Esos tres lanzamientos lentos supusieron 47 de sus 88 lanzamientos, más de la mitad de su carga de trabajo. Esa confianza en sus lanzamientos secundarios le ayudó a conseguir una tasa global de strikes fallidos del 32,6 %, sin conceder bases por bolas. La bola rápida de cuatro costuras y la sinker de la estrella de los Yankees le dieron los peores resultados, y fueron los que menos utilizó.
Ahora viene una prueba más dura.
Fried se enfrentará a los Rays la semana que viene en uno de los dos partidos de una doble jornada que dará inicio a una serie decisiva de cuatro partidos en el Yankee Stadium. Los Yankees siguen a 3 1/2 partidos del Tampa Bay (91-59) en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 11 partidos por disputar.
«Va a ser béisbol de eliminatorias», dijo Fried. «Son dos equipos, dos equipos realmente buenos, que van a darlo todo. Estoy deseando formar parte de esto y no veo la hora de que llegue la semana que viene».
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

September 16 - Spencer Jones belted a three-run home run, Cody Bellinger hammered a two-run shot, and the New York Yankees cruised to an 8-1 win over the Minnesota Twins on Tuesday in Minneapolis.
Bellinger collected three hits while Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Anthony Volpe had two apiece for New York (88-63), which earned its third win in a row and its seventh in eight games. The Yankees will look to complete a three-game sweep of the Twins on Wednesday afternoon.
Luke Keaschall went 3-for-4 and Emmanuel Rodriguez finished 2-for-3 with an RBI for Minnesota (70-81), which took its seventh loss in nine games.
Yankees left-hander Max Fried (5-4) allowed one run on six hits in seven innings. He walked none and struck out six.
Twins right-hander Bailey Ober (7-6) gave up three runs on nine hits in 5 1/3 innings. He fanned three and walked two.
The Yankees jumped to a 2-0 lead in the top of the first. Ben Rice hit a leadoff single, and Bellinger followed with a 399-foot, two-run homer over the wall in right-center field.
The Twins cut the deficit to 2-1 in the second. Royce Lewis reached on an infield single, swiped second base and scored on a single to center by Rodriguez.
Lombard put the Yankees on top 3-1 in the third with an RBI single to right.
New York broke the game open with four runs in the sixth.
Rice reached on an error, Bellinger walked and Ramos drove in Rice with a double to left.
Two batters later, Jones belted a three-run homer to center to put New York up by six runs. The 423-foot blast landed in the second deck of the outfield.
The Yankees capped the scoring in the ninth when Jose Caballero singled to center to score Lombard from second.
New York left-hander Ryan Yarbrough finished the game with two scoreless innings. He threw 21 of 29 pitches for strikes.
--Field Level Media

Baltimore, Maryland.- Paul Goldschmidt conectó un jonrón en el primer lanzamiento del partido, Trent Grisham bateó un cuadrangular de tres carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York vencieron a los Orioles de Baltimore 6-2 el martes por la noche para poner fin a una racha de cuatro derrotas consecutivas.
Will Warren (5-1) permitió dos carreras y cuatro hits en 5 2/3 entradas para los Yankees. Fue una buena actuación para el lanzador derecho, quien había permitido seis carreras en cuatro entradas a Texas en su apertura anterior.
El cuarto jonrón de apertura de Goldschmidt en su carrera y el segundo en cuatro días puso a Nueva York al frente definitivamente, y el batazo de Grisham puso el marcador 6-0 en la tercera entrada. Ambos jonrones fueron contra el zurdo Trevor Rogers, quien solo duró cuatro entradas en su regreso de la lista de lesionados tras una larga enfermedad.
En su primer partido como lanzador desde el 25 de abril, Rogers (2-4) permitió seis carreras y seis hits, elevando su efectividad a 5.77 en comparación con 1.81 en 2025.
Rogers se metió en problemas en la tercera entrada cuando otorgó dos bases por bolas consecutivas que llenaron las bases con un out. Luego, Cody Bellinger bateó un rodado que resultó en un out forzado, produciendo una carrera; Amed Rosario impulsó una carrera con un sencillo al cuadro y Grisham coronó la remontada con su sexto jonrón.
Esa ofensiva fue más que suficiente para asegurar a Nueva York su décima victoria en 11 partidos contra Baltimore, remontándonos a la temporada pasada.
Los equipos lograron superar las cuatro revisiones de decisiones arbitrales que presentaron ante el árbitro principal, Hunter Wendelstedt.
Los Yankees de Nueva York llamaron al campocorto Anthony Volpe de la filial Triple-A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre y colocaron a José Caballero en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una fractura en un dedo. Se espera que Volpe sea titular en el último partido de la serie el miércoles.
A continuación
El partido del miércoles se adelantó a las 13:05 h desde las 18:35 h debido a la amenaza de mal tiempo. Max Fried (4-2, 2.91 ERA) será el abridor por Nueva York, y Kyle Bradish (1-5, 4.83) será el probable abridor por Baltimore.

He became the second manager in MLB history to reach the postseason in at least eight of his first nine seasons, joining Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, who has now done it in each of his first 11 seasons. Boone is also the third manager to make the playoffs in eight of his first nine seasons with the Yankees, joining Joe Torre and Casey Stengel.
